questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why industry came first to Britain
questions.learningObjective: Identify why industrialization began in Britain
questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains why industrialization began in Britain before elsewhere?

options.text: Abundant coal, capital, and a growing consumer market
A large peasant population with no wage labor
options.misconception: confuses agrarian stasis with industrial take-off

options.text: Absence of any government support for trade
options.misconception: reverses Britain's mercantile and imperial policies

options.text: A climate too cold for agriculture
options.misconception: mistakes climate determinism for industrial causes

questions.explanation: Coal, capital, and consumer demand combined to spark industry. Agrarian stasis, lack of state support, and climate are not the causes.
questions.hint: Look for resources, capital, and demand.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.stem: How did factory production differ from the putting-out system?

answer.exemplar: Factories concentrated workers and machines under one roof with centralized supervision, whereas putting-out dispersed work among rural households paid by the piece.

questions.explanation: Factory production centralized labor and power; putting-out dispersed it. The change was organizational as much as technological.
questions.hint: Contrast centralization with dispersed household work.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of Watt's condenser

stimulus.body: An engine previously wasted fuel by cooling and reheating its cylinder each stroke. A new design kept the cylinder hot while condensing steam separately, cutting fuel use and making steam power economical beyond coal mines.

questions.stem: What problem did this innovation solve?

options.text: It eliminated the need for any fuel at all
It reduced fuel waste by separating condensation from the cylinder
It allowed engines to run on water instead of steam
It made engines small enough for pocket watches

questions.explanation: The separate condenser kept the cylinder hot, reducing fuel waste. It did not eliminate fuel, switch to water, or miniaturize engines.
questions.hint: Notice separation of condensation from the cylinder.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain waterpower's effect on mill siting
questions.stem: Before steam power spread, where were textile mills most likely to be located?

options.text: In dense city centers near consumer markets
options.misconception: ignores the need for flowing water

options.text: On high mountain peaks for wind power
Along fast-flowing rivers in rural areas
Inside royal palaces for protection
options.misconception: mistakes political security for industrial siting

questions.explanation: Water-powered mills needed fast-flowing rivers, often in rural areas. City centers, peaks, and palaces did not meet this need.
questions.hint: Look for flowing water and rural sites.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY

stimulus.body: Some historians argue that a sudden surge of investment and innovation around 1760 transformed Britain, while others see gradual growth stretching across the eighteenth century with no single breakthrough moment. Both sides cite rising output and changing technology.

questions.stem: What is the core disagreement in this source?

Whether Britain or France industrialized first
options.misconception: introduces a national comparison not debated here

options.text: Whether change was sudden or gradual
Whether technology or population drove change
options.misconception: adds a causal debate not raised

questions.explanation: The debate is about timing and pace, sudden versus gradual. Both sides accept industrialization and rising output.
questions.hint: Notice sudden surge versus gradual growth.

All workers became landowners

Labor supply outpaced demand or productivity gains

questions.explanation: Stagnant wages amid population growth suggests labor supply exceeded demand or productivity. Rising profits, halted growth, and universal landownership are not indicated.
questions.hint: Relate wages to labor supply and productivity.
